Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

[{"id": "arka-boost-prompt-long-0171", "row_sha256": "750d8208c5731aa403234bdfbf1fadf2da803a2021371d0c2185b9f6f2e5c83d", "mode": "/prompt", "language": "en", "context": {}, "identity": false, "mode_instructions": "Organize the supplied request into a clear prompt. Preserve scope and constraints. Do not invent context, requirements, or missing information. Do not perform the task.", "input": "hey, can you turn this into a clear prompt for drafting an email to Alder Cove Municipal Harbor about a seasonal mooring? i need to ask about a berth for my sailboat, not write as if anything has already been granted. the harbor is in Alder Cove, and my name is Lena Ortiz. The boat is Maribel, a 1988 Catalina 26, California registration CA 4821 QP. My current rental at a private dock ends June 30, so I’m looking for a municipal mooring from July 1 through October 31. The date range is what I’m asking about; it isn’t confirmed. Keep the email polite and direct, and don’t make it sound like I’m complaining about the private dock or demanding a particular spot.

some of the boat information should be included because they may need it to check fit and fees. Maribel is 26 feet overall, with an 8-foot-6-inch beam and a 4-foot-3-inch draft, and the displacement is 7,200 pounds. It has a 9.9 hp outboard. The 26 feet is the overall length, not a claim about the length of the hull alone. Please don’t round or convert the measurements. I can provide the registration and proof of insurance, but the email should not imply I’ve already sent either document. I want to ask what documents they need and when they want them, and whether the application has to be filed before the requested start date.

for the location, my first choice is the eastern basin, preferably a mooring where I can get to the public launch without crossing the work float area. I know that could be too specific or unavailable, so ask whether any seasonal space is open in the eastern basin rather than writing as though they owe me that location. A neighbor told me, “the north row gets choppy when the afternoon wind comes around”. That is just a remark I heard, not something the harbor has confirmed, and it shouldn’t be presented as an official condition. If the eastern basin has no space, I could consider a north-row mooring only if dinghy tie-up is allowed and the public launch lane would stay unobstructed. If those two things can’t be confirmed, ask what other locations or wait-list options are available; don’t say I will take the north row anyway.

I also have an 8-foot inflatable dinghy with no motor. I would need to know whether it may be tied up at the assigned mooring or must be stored somewhere else. I sometimes bring a single kayak, but I’m not asking the harbor to reserve space for it or for a second boat. Please ask whether there are rules about dinghies, kayaks, or gear near the moorings, without assuming that any of them may be left on the dock. A harbor worker I spoke with said, “Please ask before tying anything to the outer rail.” Keep that sentence as a quoted remark if it is used, and don’t turn it into a general harbor rule because I don’t know whether it applies to all slips or just that rail.

there are a couple of practical timing things worth asking about. I can come to the office on a weekday, but I need to know whether an in-person visit is required or if the application can be emailed. I work until 3 p.m. on Tuesdays and Thursdays, so if they only take applications in person, ask about a suitable time rather than promising that I can come at any hour. My regular schedule is more open on Wednesdays and Fridays. I expect to use the boat on weekends and some weekday evenings, but I’m not asking for special access or after-hours service. Ask whether there are normal check-in or key arrangements for a mooring holder.

include these office notes exactly as written, since I copied them from the harbor information page: “Office hours: Tuesday–Friday, 9:00 a.m.–4:00 p.m.” “Seasonal rate: not listed on the website.” “Bring proof of insurance and current registration when submitting an application.” Don’t guess the price from another harbor, and don’t state that the last note means my documents have already been accepted. I need the prompt to ask the office to confirm the current seasonal fee, any deposit or separate launch fee, and the payment deadline. The web page doesn’t say the rate, so the email should ask rather than suggest a number.

there’s also a separate comment from the harbor coordinator, not a promise about a space: “We can hold the outer finger until the tide turns, but not promise it past Friday.” I heard that while asking a general question, and I don’t know whether it refers to this application, a different berth, or a temporary arrangement. If it matters, the email can politely ask whether it applies to seasonal moorings and what “past Friday” refers to, but it must not claim I have a hold. Don’t blend that comment with the office notes or change its wording.

please ask about the application process, availability for the full July 1–October 31 period, total charges and deadlines, required documents, and any inspection or vessel-fit requirements. I’d like a reply by email if possible, but don’t give them an invented deadline to answer. If the requested period is unavailable, ask whether there is a wait list or a shorter period worth discussing. Don’t request a reservation before the office confirms the terms, and don’t say I accept an alternate mooring. The email can close by thanking them and offering to send the registration and insurance information after they tell me how to apply. Keep it to a normal-length email rather than a formal letter, and organize the prompt so another writer can see which facts are established, which are questions, and what conditional alternative I’m willing to consider.

1) One final detail: the public launch is on the east side of the harbor, and I use it to move the dinghy, not to launch Maribel. Don’t imply that Maribel is trailered or that I need trailer storage. I’m not asking for a slip, winter storage, electrical service, or a permanent year-round mooring. Keep the request limited to a seasonal mooring and related application information. The point is to ask clearly about availability and practical terms while leaving the decision to the harbor office.

Please keep the final part of the prompt about that limited scope; don’t drop it just because the application and fee questions come earlier. The overall result should direct the email writer to be courteous, accurate, and reasonably concise, with no assumed approval, no made-up fee, and no commitment to a conditional alternative.", "output": "Create a polite, direct, normal-length email to Alder Cove Municipal Harbor asking about a seasonal mooring. Do not write as though a mooring has been granted, a space is being held, or the harbor has confirmed any of the details that remain uncertain. Keep the request courteous rather than demanding or critical of the sender’s current dock.

### Sender and vessel
The sender is Lena Ortiz. Her sailboat is Maribel, a 1988 Catalina 26, California registration CA 4821 QP. She is seeking a municipal mooring from July 1 through October 31 because her current private-dock rental ends June 30. This is the period she is asking about, not a confirmed booking.

Include the vessel details without rounding or converting them: 26 feet overall, 8-foot-6-inch beam, 4-foot-3-inch draft, 7,200 pounds displacement, and a 9.9 hp outboard. The 26 feet is the overall length, not a stated hull-only length. Lena can provide current registration and proof of insurance, but has not sent them. Ask what documents are required, when they are due, and whether the application must be filed before the requested start date.

### Location and related equipment
Ask whether a seasonal space is available in the eastern basin. Lena’s preference is a mooring from which she can reach the public launch without crossing the work float area, but do not imply that a particular location is owed or available. The public launch is on the east side of the harbor. Lena uses it to move her dinghy, not to launch Maribel; do not imply that Maribel is trailered or that trailer storage is needed.

A neighbor said, “the north row gets choppy when the afternoon wind comes around”. This is an unconfirmed remark, not an official harbor condition. Lena would consider a north-row mooring only if dinghy tie-up is allowed and the public launch lane would remain unobstructed. If both points cannot be confirmed, ask about other locations or wait-list options; do not say that Lena will accept the north row regardless.

Lena has an 8-foot inflatable dinghy with no motor and sometimes brings one kayak. She is not asking for space for a second boat or for the kayak to be reserved. Ask whether dinghies, kayaks, or gear are subject to rules and whether the dinghy may be tied at the assigned mooring or must be stored elsewhere. Do not assume that equipment may be left on the dock. If relevant, retain this remark exactly as quoted: “Please ask before tying anything to the outer rail.” It came from a harbor worker, and Lena does not know whether it applies to all slips or only that rail; do not present it as a general harbor rule.

### Application, fees, and timing
Ask about availability for the full July 1–October 31 period, the application process, required documents, any inspection or vessel-fit requirements, total charges, and deadlines. Ask the office to confirm the current seasonal fee, any deposit or separate launch fee, and the payment deadline. Do not guess a price or imply that the documents have been received or accepted.

Include these copied office notes exactly as written:
“Office hours: Tuesday–Friday, 9:00 a.m.–4:00 p.m.”
“Seasonal rate: not listed on the website.”
“Bring proof of insurance and current registration when submitting an application.”

Lena can visit on a weekday but needs to know whether an in-person visit is required or whether the application can be emailed. She works until 3 p.m. on Tuesdays and Thursdays and is more available on Wednesdays and Fridays. If an in-person application is required, ask about a suitable time; do not promise that she can come at any hour. She expects to use the boat on weekends and some weekday evenings, but is not requesting special access or after-hours service. Ask whether ordinary check-in or key arrangements apply to a mooring holder.

The harbor coordinator made this separate comment: “We can hold the outer finger until the tide turns, but not promise it past Friday.” Lena does not know whether it concerns this application, another berth, or a temporary arrangement. Do not describe it as a hold or a promise. If useful, politely ask whether the comment applies to seasonal moorings and what “past Friday” refers to. Keep the comment separate from the copied office notes and preserve its wording exactly.

### Alternatives and closing
If the requested period is unavailable, ask whether there is a wait list or a shorter period worth discussing. Do not request a reservation before the office confirms the terms, and do not say Lena accepts an alternate mooring. Ask for a reply by email if possible, without imposing an invented response deadline. The email may close by thanking the office and offering to send registration and insurance information after Lena is told how to apply.

Keep the request limited to a seasonal mooring and related application information. Lena is not asking for a slip, winter storage, electrical service, or a permanent year-round mooring. Close the email in a courteous, concise manner, leaving the decision to the harbor office and making no unsupported claims about approval, fees, or location."}]
